draft.title: Domain and range notation
card: An interval is a set of numbers between two ends. A square bracket [ or ] includes the end number. A round bracket ( or ) leaves it out.
Example: [0, 5) means all numbers from 0 up to but not including 5. So 0 is in the interval and 5 is not.
The symbol ∞ means the numbers go on without end. It is not a number, so it always gets a round bracket, as in [0, ∞).
A restricted domain is written f: [0, ∞) → R. This reads: f is a function whose inputs are x ≥ 0, and whose outputs are real numbers. For f(x) = x² on this domain, the range is [0, ∞).
draft.remember: Square bracket includes the end. Round bracket leaves it out. Infinity always gets a round bracket.

a.q: Which interval contains every x with −2 < x ≤ 3?
a.why: −2 is not included, so it gets a round bracket. 3 is included, so it gets a square bracket. [−2, 3] is tempting, but it wrongly includes −2.
a.clue: Check each end on its own: is it included or not?

b.q: A function is f: [1, ∞) → R, where f(x) = x². Which input is NOT allowed?
b.why: The domain [1, ∞) holds only numbers from 1 upwards, with 1 included. So 0 is outside it and is not allowed. x = 1 is allowed because the square bracket includes 1.
b.clue: The domain is the set of allowed inputs, not the outputs.

final.title: Domain and range notation
card: An interval is a set of numbers between two ends. A square bracket [ or ] includes the end number. A round bracket ( or ) leaves it out.
Example: \([0, 5)\) means all numbers from 0 up to but not including 5. So 0 is in the interval and 5 is not.
The symbol \(\infty\) means the numbers go on without end. It is not a number, so it always gets a round bracket, as in \([0, \infty)\).

A restricted domain is written \(f: [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\). This reads: \(f\) is a function whose inputs are \(x \ge 0\), and whose outputs are real numbers. For \(f(x) = x^{2}\) on this domain, the range is \([0, \infty)\).
final.remember: Square bracket includes the end. Round bracket leaves it out. Infinity always gets a round bracket.

a.q: Which interval contains every \(x\) with \(-2 < x \le 3\)?
a.why: \(-2\) is not included, so it gets a round bracket. 3 is included, so it gets a square bracket. \([-2, 3]\) is tempting, but it wrongly includes \(-2\).
a.clue: Check each end on its own: is it included or not?

b.q: A function is \(f: [1, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\), where \(f(x) = x^{2}\). Which input is NOT allowed?
b.why: The domain \([1, \infty)\) holds only numbers from 1 upwards, with 1 included. So 0 is outside it and is not allowed. \(x = 1\) is allowed because the square bracket includes 1.
b.clue: The domain is the set of allowed inputs, not the outputs.
